title: A schoolteacher's number puzzle
teaches: Why each kind of atom gives out and soaks up only certain colours: Balmer's pattern, Bohr's ladder, and the electron as a wave

blocks.text: In 1885 **Johann Balmer** was sixty, and he taught mathematics at a girls' secondary school in Basel. He had published a little on geometry and on the proportions of the Temple in Ezekiel's vision, and he enjoyed number puzzles. A friend at the university, the physicist Eduard Hagenbach, told him he had a good one.

Hydrogen, heated in a tube until it glows, gives out light of exactly four colours that the eye can see: a red, a blue-green, and two violets. The Swedish physicist Anders Ångström had measured them with great care. In nanometres (millionths of a millimetre), they were 656.3, 486.1, 434.0 and 410.2. Here, in a list of four numbers, was the simplest atom there is, writing its signature. Was there a pattern?

Balmer found one. Take a single number, 364.56. Multiply it by 9/5 and you get the red line. By 4/3, the blue-green. By 25/21 and 9/8, the two violets. Written out to show the pattern, the fractions are 9/5, 16/12, 25/21 and 36/32: on top, the squares of 3, 4, 5 and 6; underneath, each square less 4. Every line came out right to within a part in ten thousand.

A pattern that fits four numbers you already have might be a coincidence. So Balmer did the honest thing and made a prediction. The next square is 49, so there should be a fifth line at 364.56 × 49/45, about 397 nm, just at the violet edge of sight, and more after it, crowding closer and closer together toward 364.56 itself. Hagenbach told him that photographs of white stars, which show the ultraviolet the eye can't, already showed a run of hydrogen lines beyond the four. They sat where Balmer's rule said they would.

blocks.caption: Hydrogen's lines in Balmer's arrangement. The four Ångström measured are bright; the pale ones are those his rule predicted, crowding toward a limit at 364.56 nm.

blocks.text: What Balmer could not say was why. His rule was a key that fitted a lock, found by a man who had no idea what was inside the door. It sat in the textbooks for twenty-eight years, accurate and unexplained.

parts.title: An atom that should not last

blocks.text: Meanwhile people were finding out what an atom is. In 1897 J. J. Thomson in Cambridge found the **electron**, a particle far lighter than any atom, with a negative electric charge, that could be pulled out of any kind of matter. Atoms, then, had parts. In 1911 **Ernest Rutherford** in Manchester had his students fire fast, positively charged particles from radium at a sheet of gold leaf about a thousand atoms thick. Nearly all went straight through. About one in eight thousand bounced back. “It was quite the most incredible event that has ever happened to me in my life,” he said later. “It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.”

The only way to bounce a heavy, fast particle straight back is to hit something heavier still, and small. So almost all of an atom's mass sits in a tiny, positively charged **nucleus** at its middle, about a hundred-thousandth of the atom's width. Scale a gold atom up to the size of a football stadium and the nucleus is a pea on the centre spot. The electrons are somewhere out in the stands. The rest is empty. (The nucleus is itself made of **protons**, which carry its charge, and, as was found in 1932, **neutrons**, which carry none. Hydrogen's nucleus is a single proton.)

This lovely picture had a fatal flaw. Opposite charges attract, so the electron must move round the nucleus to keep from falling in, like a planet round the Sun. But an electric charge that swings round sends out waves, which is how a radio aerial works, and the waves carry energy away. By the physics everyone trusted, an orbiting electron should spiral into the nucleus, glowing as it fell, in about a hundred-billionth of a second, giving a smear of every colour on the way down. Every atom in the universe should have collapsed long ago. They haven't, and when they do glow, they give sharp lines, not smears.

**Niels Bohr** was a young Dane who had spent part of 1912 with Rutherford in Manchester, and went home to Copenhagen worrying at the collapsing atom. Early in 1913 a colleague asked him whether he knew Balmer's formula. He didn't, and looked it up. “As soon as I saw Balmer's formula,” he said later, “the whole thing was immediately clear to me.”

What Bohr did was not so much explain the atom as lay down the law to it. An electron in an atom, he said, can only be on certain levels, like the rungs of a ladder. While it sits on one it gives out nothing, whatever the old physics says. It can jump from a higher rung to a lower one, and when it does, it gives out one packet of light (Planck's packets, from *Why are there no green stars?*) carrying exactly the energy of the gap. A packet's energy fixes its colour: a big drop gives a blue or ultraviolet packet, a small drop a red or infrared one. An atom can only give out the colours that match the gaps in its ladder.

Then came the part that convinced people. Bohr worked out where hydrogen's rungs would have to be, using only the electron's charge and mass and Planck's constant, numbers measured for quite other reasons. The rungs crowd closer together as they go up, and fall off to nothing at the top, where the electron is free. The gaps he found gave Balmer's 364.56 to within the accuracy of the measurements. A schoolteacher's number had been built out of the parts of the atom.

blocks.caption: Hydrogen's ladder of energy, to scale, with the bottom rung at the foot and the electron free at the top. Each fall between two rungs gives one packet of light; the colour is set by the size of the fall.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then find falls that give all four of hydrogen's visible lines

blocks.text: All four visible lines are falls that end on the second rung. Balmer's squares were the squares of the rung numbers all along: his 9, 16, 25 and 36 are rungs 3 to 6, and the 4 he took away is rung 2 squared. Falls that end on the bottom rung are much bigger, and their packets are all ultraviolet; Theodore Lyman found them in 1906. Falls that end on rung 3 are small and give infrared, which Friedrich Paschen found in 1908. Bohr's ladder had room for both before anyone told him about them.

The ladder runs both ways. An electron on a low rung can be lifted to a higher one, but only by a packet of light that carries exactly the energy of the gap. A packet with a little more or a little less goes past untouched. So a gas soaks up from passing light exactly the colours it would give out when glowing. That is Kirchhoff's rule from *What the stars are made of*, the reason a cool gas in front of a lamp prints dark lines in the same places as its bright ones. The tuned bell of that lesson has turned out to be a ladder.

Lift an electron right off the top of the ladder and it is free: the atom has lost an electron, and is said to be **ionised**. An ionised hydrogen atom is a bare proton, with no ladder at all, so it can neither absorb nor give out lines. That will matter in *Mostly hydrogen*, where it explains why the hottest stars hardly seem to have any hydrogen.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: An electron in an atom can only be on certain rungs of energy. A fall gives out one packet of light whose colour is set by the size of the fall; a packet with exactly that energy can lift it back up.
Hydrogen's four visible lines are the falls that end on its second rung.

parts.title: Why there are rungs at all

blocks.text: Bohr's rule worked, but it was a decree, not a reason. Why should an electron be allowed on some rungs and not between them? The answer came in 1924, in the doctoral thesis of **Louis de Broglie**, a French aristocrat who had switched from history to physics. Light, Einstein had shown, is a wave that comes in packets. De Broglie turned it around: perhaps a particle like the electron is also a wave.

Pluck a guitar string. It is held at both ends, so it can only vibrate in patterns that fit: one half-wave along its length, or two, or three, but never two and a half. That is why a string has a note and its overtones, and nothing in between. An electron held by its nucleus is a wave held in, and only certain patterns fit there too. Each pattern has its own energy. Those are the rungs.

blocks.caption: The ways a string held at both ends can vibrate: whole numbers of half-waves, and nothing between. An electron held in an atom has only certain patterns, and so only certain energies.

blocks.text: The examiners were baffled, and the thesis was sent to Einstein, who liked it. Within three years Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer in New York, firing electrons at a crystal of nickel, saw them spread out in the pattern only waves make. By then Erwin Schrödinger had written down the rule such waves obey, and the rungs came out of it exactly, without Bohr's decree. The electron in an atom is not really a little planet on an orbit at all. It is a standing wave, a cloud of where it might be found, with a shape fixed by its rung.

Hydrogen has one electron and a simple ladder. Iron has twenty-six electrons, and its ladder is a tangle of thousands of rungs, which is why iron prints thousands of lines across the Sun's spectrum. But every element has its own ladder, and so its own lines, as fixed as a fingerprint. That is why the spectroscope could answer Comte, who had said nobody would ever know what the stars are made of. It also means that which lines a star shows depends on which rungs its electrons are sitting on, and that depends on how hot it is. Cecilia Payne would make a great deal of that.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the ladder inside the atom
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: An electron falls from rung 6 to rung 2 in one hydrogen atom, and from rung 3 to rung 2 in another. Which packet of light is bluer?
items.why: Rung 6 is higher, so the fall is bigger and the packet carries more energy. More energy means a bluer colour: 410 nm against 656 nm.

items.ask: Why did Rutherford's atom, with electrons orbiting a tiny nucleus, look impossible by the physics of 1911?
choices: An orbiting charge should radiate away its energy and spiral in
The nucleus was too small to hold anything
Electrons were too light to orbit
items.why: A charge that swings round sends out waves and loses energy, like a radio aerial. The electron should have spiralled in at once, smearing out every colour.

items.ask: A cool cloud of hydrogen sits in front of a hot star. Which colours does it take out of the starlight?
choices: The same colours hydrogen gives out when it glows
The colours hydrogen never gives out
items.why: Only a packet with exactly the energy of a gap can lift an electron up the ladder, and those are the same gaps it falls across when glowing.

items.ask: Falls that end on hydrogen's bottom rung give light that is:
choices: Ultraviolet: the gaps down to rung 1 are big
Infrared: the gaps down to rung 1 are small
Red, like the brightest visible line
items.why: The bottom rung lies far below the others, so any fall to it is large and gives a packet too energetic to see. Lyman found them in 1906.

items.ask: Why was Balmer's prediction of a fifth line a better test than his fit to the first four?
choices: Any pattern can be made to fit numbers you already have; a prediction can fail
Because the fifth line was red
Because Ångström had measured it more carefully
items.why: With enough ingenuity you can find a rule for any four numbers. A rule that tells you where to look for something new, and is right, is much harder to fake.

items.ask: In de Broglie's picture, why can an electron in an atom have only certain energies?
choices: It is a wave held in, and only certain wave patterns fit
The nucleus allows only certain speeds
Light can only come in certain colours
items.why: Like a guitar string held at both ends, a wave held round the nucleus can only vibrate in whole-number patterns, each with its own energy: the rungs.

summary: **Balmer found a rule without a reason.** In 1885 one number, 364.56 nm, times 9/5, 16/12, 25/21 and 36/32, gave hydrogen's four visible lines, and it predicted more that were then found.
**An atom is mostly empty.** Rutherford's bounced particles showed a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus with electrons far outside it.
**By the old physics, atoms should collapse.** An orbiting electron should radiate and spiral in, giving a smear of colour, not sharp lines.
**Bohr's ladder.** An electron can only be on certain rungs; a fall between two gives one packet of light whose colour is set by the size of the fall.
**Hydrogen's visible lines all end on the second rung.** Falls to the bottom rung give ultraviolet, falls to the third give infrared.

**Absorbing is the same jump upward.** A gas soaks up exactly the colours it gives out, so its dark lines and bright lines fall in the same places. Knock an electron off the top and the atom is ionised.
**The rungs exist because the electron is a wave.** Like a string held at both ends, a wave held round a nucleus fits only certain patterns, each with its own energy.
